Senses.Explanation: To stand with one’s head against heaven and feet on earth is the record’s epithet for a person presented as fully standing on their own. Masters apply it to the person within a monastery’s scene, to traveling monks carrying staffs, and to the one who can withstand direct testing without retreating into excuses. Feiyin Tongrong answers “what is the person within Huangbo’s scene?” with “head against heaven and feet on earth,” making the phrase a direct portrait-answer. Lianfeng Su addresses the “superior one who investigates Chan” as iron-headed, copper-browed, and standing between heaven and earth before describing blows and reversals that do not move him. Sanyi Mingyu pairs the phrase with having neither a tile overhead nor room below for an awl, while an unnamed monk in Lingji Xingguan’s record uses it to challenge why so many people are buried alive. Juelang Daosheng makes the status conditional: only one who can pass through the successive shouts is allowed to be such a person. The phrase is therefore an epithet tested in public speech, not a physical measurement.
